arbol_de_trazas.nota: El árbol lo arman el `EjecutorDeEtapas` (corrida y etapa) y el decorador de puertos (una traza por llamada a puerto). **Ninguna etapa emite su propio span** — la observabilidad lo prohíbe y señala al ejecutor como el lugar correcto para el desglose. `campos_censurados > 0` es el registro de decisiones actuando: en una consulta ad-hoc no viaja ni el pedido ni la imagen.

politica.por_que: Las 30 consultas de evaluación se trazan **completas** (`el registro de decisiones la política de trazado`). No son dato de un tercero: son obras de nuestro propio held-out, versionadas con el ground truth porque son el **instrumento de medición** (el registro de decisiones). Trazarlas enteras cumple las técnicas avanzadas aisladas por medición, la tabla de tokens, costo y la figura y el criterio de costo sin tocar el compromiso de privacidad.

entrada.nota_de_retencion: el registro de decisiones (cierra la pregunta por el ciclo de vida de la corrida purgada): **no se persiste nada de un tercero**. Los bytes de la imagen no se guardan nunca —no hay clave que los active— y el `pedido` solo si `[retencion] pedido = true`. Lo que se vacía son **campos**, y que estaban vaciados queda registrado (la regla de qué se versiona): la corrida conserva su `corrida_id`, su ordinal, sus rankings y sus degradaciones, porque borrarla reasignaría el ordinal y un informe que cita la corrida #1 apuntaría a otra ejecución.

aic:210482.texto:
This architectural rendering of a magnificent tomb at Agra provides an accurate depiction of the semiprecious stones inlaid in white marble, a technique known as pietra dura, and the carved white marble jali screens of the mausoleum built by the Mughal empress Nur Jahan (1577–1645). She commissioned this building in honor of her father, Mirza Ghiyas Beg, who rose to become the prime minister under the emperor Jahangir (reigned 1605–27) and held the exalted title I’timad-ud-Daula (Pillar of the Empire). The powerful Nur Jahan had immense financial resources at her disposal. Built between 1622 and 1628 and modest in size, as befitted the mausoleum of a nobleman rather than an emperor, the structure is unique in its lavish epigraphic and decorative design, highlighting its exquisite quality and craftsmanship.
This drawing was created in the Company style, named after the British East India Company, which led English mercantile and political interests in the subcontinent from the early seventeenth to the mid-nineteenth century. British colonists were eager to record and catalogue everything they saw. In the absence of photography, British and Indian artists depicted the sights in finely detailed prints and drawings. The style arose in the later part of the eighteenth century and ended in the mid-nineteenth with the beginning of photography. In addition to rendering architectural drawings, artists working in the Company style also produced animal and botanical studies and images of Indian occupations and trades, regional dress, festivals, and scenes of village life.
aic:210482.title: I'timad-ud-Daula's Tomb at Agra

cma:146196.texto:
The Sat Sai is a poetry collection describing the 
beauty of women in a range of emotional states. 
The heroine of this poem sits against a tree that is 
in full flower. Not coincidentally, her dress matches 
the color of the blossoms, but no bees come to 
pollinate. Her lover is absent, and other girls walk 
by, gossiping.

The oval format was inspired by British art. 
The scene is from a poem written for a king in 
northwestern India by an author from eastern 
India, who was raised in a north Indian city. This 
painting reveals the movement of art and poets 
across multiple regions.
cma:146196.title: The lovelorn heroine, from a Sat Sai of Bihari

cma:163582.texto:
The Mughal emperor responsible for a revival of courtly arts and pastimes was Muhammad Shah (reigned 1719–48). This painting was made by an artist from a small kingdom in the western Himalayas who stayed at the Mughal court in Delhi and painted scenes of his experiences. 

Like his predecessors, Muhammad Shah enjoyed watching elephant fights. He is shown in his window of public audience, marked by a golden carpet, smoking a hookah. Women from his harem can be seen looking on from behind painted screens.

Two pairs of men hold fire brands and spears to prevent the elephants from running off and to keep them under control. The intensity of the fight—captured at a moment when one mahout, or elephant trainer, has dropped his goad and is about to jump off—is augmented by the dense colors and forms in contrast to the otherwise pale planes, balanced only by the strip of palace windows.
cma:163582.title: Two Elephants Fighting in a Courtyard Before Muhammad Shah

cma:314237.texto: One woman is gently washing the right foot of the lady. This composition is based on a Mughal painting.
cma:314237.title: Palace women enjoy music by the side of a cascade

cma:314237.texto: Sitting by an artificial cascade in a palace, a woman smokes a hookah and enjoys a music performance with her attendants. She raises her left hand in appreciation of the musicians and turns toward a companion (sakhi) who also shares her enthusiasm. Three attendants stand behind her—one holding a box of betel leaves, while the other two hold a fly whisk and a fan.

cma:438621.texto: This painting is from the earliest known Jain series made in a Mughal-inspired style.
cma:438621.title: Prince Shreyamsa dreams of the coming of Rishabha, from a Panchakalyanaka (Five Auspicious Events)

cma:438621.texto:
Dreams foretell important events in Indian literature. In this painting a prince lies half asleep and experiences eight visions, pictured above the reclining figure. At the right, the prince on the throne with the royal umbrella seeks help interpreting the dreams. They predicted the coming of Rishabha, the first Jina, who has been fasting for a full year. The prince then became the first person in the world to give proper alms, or pious offerings, to a Jina.
 
This painting is from a group that is recognized as the first Jain manuscript made in the form of a pictorial series, rather than a handwritten manuscript.
cma:438621.title: Prince Shreyamsa dreams of the coming of Rishabha, from a Panchakalyanaka (Five Auspicious Events)

salida.nota_de_idioma: el contrato de la salida citada / el criterio de idioma: la explicación en **español**, el fragmento citado **textual en inglés, sin traducir**. Instrumentando en el **`EjecutorDeEtapas`**, que es el lugar que ese mismo recuadro señala, **sí hay latencia para las ocho**. la latencia por etapa deja de estar sobre-prometido. **Va reportado.**

nota_de_a8_vs_bd4: 🔴 **Las dos lecturas del libro mayor, y son proyecciones del mismo dato**: la tabla de costo pide el gasto *por etapa* y la atribución de cada llamada lo cuenta *por rol, no por el nombre de la etapa*. En C1–C3 son **1:1**; en C4 el reranker es **N llamadas de un rol y una etapa** y `embedding_texto` es **un rol en dos etapas**. `libro_mayor` agrupa por rol —que sigue siendo la atribución de registro, declarada por el binding— y `libro_mayor_por_etapa` por la etapa en que el span corrió, **derivada del árbol de trazas y no de un parámetro**. Los totales coinciden por construcción: son dos `GROUP BY` de la misma lista de spans, no dos acumuladores — dos acumuladores serían el **modo de falla 1** sobre la cifra de costo que se publica.
nota_de_identidad: Clase 2 (la tabla de identidades): *registro de una ejecución*. La identidad fija **las entradas, no la salida** —una salida no determinista con la misma entrada es el dato que el muestreo fijado, registrado y con su variabilidad medida mide—, así que lleva **ordinal** y la regla de que un id determina su contenido no aplica. El ordinal se **reserva** creando el directorio de forma exclusiva: `1 + n` es un *leer, después escribir* y el barrido es paralelo.
nota_de_la_tabla: degradación/la regla de qué corridas agregan a la tabla: una corrida con degradación **no planificada** no agrega a la tabla C0–C4 —*una C4 que degradó en silencio entraría etiquetada como C4 comportándose como C3*— y una con degradación **planificada** tampoco: es el criterio de respuesta garantizada y se reporta aparte. Una etapa **ausente por configuración** no degrada: no corre, y por eso C0–C3 sí agregan.

El `config_id` hashea la configuración resuelta **menos** las claves de arriba —layout, parámetros de máquina, ruteo, transporte y el precio declarado—, que son **procedencia**: viajan enteras en `configuracion_resuelta` y no mueven la identidad. Antes de esta versión el `config_id` hasheaba todo, y por eso se movió **dos veces** por claves que no cambian nada de lo que el pipeline produce, huerfanando las corridas las dos veces.
